name: Arthur Collins Redfearn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47335/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. The application was brought by Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant was represented by Mr Mitchells Solicitors, a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The United Kingdom Government (”the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [ PERSON] of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The BNP only extended membership to white nationals. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against. The racial grounds relied on were those of the passengers and employees of Serco who were of [NRP] origin. After taking legal advice Serco summarily dismissed him on [DATE_TIME]. Serco cited, inter alia, potential health and safety risks as the applicant’s continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among passengers and their carers. It also expressed concern that the applicant's continued employment could jeopardise its reputation and possibly. lead to the loss of its contract with Bradford City Council. The Employment Tribunal gave judgment on [DATE_TIME]. It noted Serco's concerns that the applicant’s continued employment might lead to difficulties with other employees and damage its relationship with the unions. The Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. His appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly. Serco was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle. Serco would apply the same approach to a member of a similar political party, which confined its membership to black people. Mr [PERSON] cannot credibly make a claim of direct race discrimination by Serco against him on the ground that he is white. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision (see paragraph 28 above). However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. The Court of Appeal ruled that Serco was not entitled to make a claim under the [DATE_TIME] Act. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The Court of appeal ruled that no case of indirect discrimination has been made out. The case was heard at the High Court in London, and the decision was made for the court of appeal to hear the case at a later date. Click here for more information on the case and its outcome. The case originated in an application (no. 47335/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). At the end of the case, the Court rules in favour of the applicant. The case was heard by the Lord Chief Justice and Mr Justice Leveson, both of whom will deliver their verdicts on December 21, 2014. The BNP only extended membership to white nationals. 70-80 percent of Serco's customer base and 35 percent of its workforce are of [NRP] origin. UNISON asked that Serco take immediate action to ensure its members were not subjected to racial hatred. Serco cited, inter alia, potential health and safety risks as the applicant’s continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among passengers and their carers. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. The racial grounds relied on were those of the passengers and employees of Serie who were of [ NRP) origin. The Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The Tribunal also dismissed the. claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means. of achieving a legitimate aim, namely the maintenance of health and. safety. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On [DATE_TIME] Serco was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. Mr [PERSON] cannot credibly make a claim of direct race discrimination by Serco against him on the ground that he is white by relying on the decision of his own chosen political party to limit its membership to white people. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution. A provision of ‘membership of the BNP’ could not be applied to a person who was not of the same colour as Mr [Person] because only persons of thesame colour as him (white) are eligible to be members of BNP. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision. However, it is formulated too narrowly to be meaningful. Court of Appeal said the Act does not assist Mr [PERSON] in this case. He is not entitled to make a claim under it as Serco is not a public authority. No case of indirect discrimination has been made out, the court said. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights for legal advice. The application was denied on the grounds that it would have had a ‘devastating’ effect on human rights, the Court of Appeal ruled. The appeal was adjourned until next week at the earliest. The case originated in an application (no. 47335/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. The application was examined at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was represented by Mr [PERSON] of Mitchells Solicitors, a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr  of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. On [DATE_TIME] UNISON, the public sector workers’ trade union, sent a letter to Serco stating that many of its members found the applicant’s continued employment a ‘significant cause for concern’ The letter advised Serco that 70-80 percent of its customer base and 35 percent of Its workforce were of [NRP] origin. Serco cited, inter alia, potential health and safety risks as the applicant's continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among passengers and their carers. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. The racial grounds relied on were those of the passengers and employees of Serco who were of (NRP) origin. He lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal. Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. Tribunal also dismissed claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, namely the maintenance of safety. Serco was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. On [DATE_TIME] his appeal was upheld on the grounds that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Mr [PERSON] cannot credibly make a claim of direct race discrimination by Serco against him on the ground that he is white. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision. However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation. All such political activists would be at the same disadvantage, whatever colour they were. The Court of Appeal ruled that Serco was not entitled to make a claim under the [DATE_TIME] Act as it was not a public authority. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. Mr [PERSON] was denied permission to appeal the decision to the Court of appeal. The appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court on a technicality. The case was referred to the High Court by the applicant's lawyer. It is not known if Mr PERSON will be allowed to appeal against the decision. The application was heard by a judge at the London High Court who ruled in favour of Serco. The Appeal Court was told by Serco that they would be able to appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3084/07) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was decided by the Court of Arbitration in Vienna on 1 July 2013. The verdict was handed down on 6 August 2013. The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the [PERSON] centre. Only the victim is still before the courts. She claims a blind-drunk security officer abused his authority in the centre in order to rape her. Now she faces trial for defamation. A few fellow [NRP], as well as the campaigning lawyer W.R. and his colleague, are continuing to stand by her. ‘Otherwise I would have killed myself’, says [Person]. It’s difficult to know where to begin in this case. With the then Interior Minister who, while the proceedings were in progress, told the National Assembly that the woman’ Claims of sexual exploitation by security staff at Caritas centre. Women told of being attacked by drunken nightwatchmen. Claimed they were paid for quick sex by pimps. Interior Ministry stated at the time that the police were confronted with a ‘wall of silence’ Judge would no longer ‘refute’ the suggestion that [PERSON] was just a 'prostitute’ – although not even the accused security officer claimed that that was the case. With a thousand asylum seekers, the centre is hopelessly over­crowded. Another hundred arrive every day. The Interior Ministry is coming under political pressure and discredits Caritas. The woman describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. Disturbing errors occur. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. The police officers at times refer to [PERSON] not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. Police officers refer to the woman as a ‘nigger’ and ‘ Nigger Woman’. The man who claims to have had intercourse with the woman claims it was entirely consensual. However, he doesn’t recognise [Person] in photo. The Wiener Neustadt Public Prosecutor’s Office, which sees the [NRP] from Traiskirchen most often in connection with drug dealing, wants to discontinue the scheme. ‘Maybe she thought she’d be given asylum sooner’ speculates the security officer. He had offered to buy the woman a drink in the bakery [DATE_TIME]. She had stroked his back and ‘cosied up’ to him. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She is not a whore. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. The trial with judges and lay assessors before Wiener Neustadt Criminal Court does not last long. No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge [PERSON] acquits the security officer. Court of Appeal finds in the woman's favour and orders the Justice Ministry to prosecute the security Officer. ‘It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of [Person],’ says the court. 'Clear proof’ that the bakery employees got her age wrong by [DATE_TIME], says the Court of appeal. 'The difficulty of correctly estimating the age of persons with a different skin colour is known' ‘These have no evidentiary value’ according to Judge [PERSON] Why not? Because the accused said that the underpants had been ‘beige’ Not another word from the detectives who had been faced with a crying, completely intimidated woman. No mention of the fact that the security officer himself admitted locking [Person] in [the room] and removing the key. Not a single line about the predicament in which female asylum seekers found themselves at the time. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. According to principal public prosecutor, ‘After [the] acquittal we have no choice but to initiate proceedings’ The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment. The judge had no doubt about the woman’s guilt. The applicant company sought the disqualification of Judge [PERSON], the judge assigned to the media proceedings, for bias. The president of the Vienna Regional Court dismissed the motion on [DATE_TIME] and held that the issue raised by the applicant was not sufficient to give rise to doubt that the judge would not decide the case objectively. It considered that by publishing the impugned statements it had merely expressed criticism, protected by the freedom of speech. It had not concerned the acquittal itself but rather the way in which the victim of the crime had been treated. The Regional Court found that the impugned statements had constituted defamation under Article 111 of the Criminal Code. It held that [PERSON] was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR) The judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced, whereas the rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. train_texts: Four Swedish nationals applied to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was later transferred to the Fifth Section, following the re-composition of the Court’s sections on [Date_TIME]. For distributing the leaflets, the applicants were charged with agitation against a national or ethnic group (hets mot folkgrupp). The applicants disputed that the text in the leaflets expressed contempt for homosexuals. They stated that the purpose of their activity had been to start a debate about the lack of objectivity in the education dispensed in [NRP] schools. The applicants requested the court to reject the charges, to consider the criminal act minor, or at least to reduce the punishments. The prosecutor appealed as regards the first three applicants, requesting the court for aggravated punishment. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicants and sentenced them to community service. The Supreme Court convicted the applicants of agitation against a national or ethnic group. The applicants disputed the appeal on the ground that a conviction would amount to a violation of their right to freedom of expression as guaranteed by the Convention. The purpose of the handing out of the leaflets was indeed to initiate a debate between pupils and teachers on a question of public interest, namely the objectivity of the education in [NRP] schools. However, these were formulated in a way that was offensive and disparaging for homosexuals as a group and in violation of the duty under Article 10 to avoid as far as possible statements that are unwarrantably offensive to others thus constituting an assault on their rights, and without contributing to any form of public debate. The first three applicants were given suspended sentences combined with fines ranging from SEK 1,800 (approximately 200 euros (EUR) to SEK 19,000 (approximately EUR 2,000) and the fourth applicant was sentenced to probation. The minority (two judges) found that convicting the applicants would not be proportionate to the aims pursued and would therefore be in violation of Article 10 of the Convention. One of them was of the view that the prosecution was not formulated in such a way that the Supreme Court could take into consideration that the leaflets had been distributed at a school and addressed to the pupils. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2010/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been unreasonable delay in enforcing the financial obligations of her ex-partner in respect of child support. The Court declared the application partly admissible as. regarded the applicant’s complaint of lack of access to court, inadmissible as regarded. her children. The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations. Mr [PERSON] returned the MEF accepting paternity. Insufficient information was given to allow a full maintenance assessment to be made. The CSA negotiated an agreement with Mr K that he would pay under the IMA, GBP 124.33 per week plus GBP 25.67 towards arrears. Mr K’s liability changed many times after that date, inter alia as his employment changed and it proved difficult to obtain information. A liability order was applied for because he had breached the agreement. The order was discontinued when regular payments were resumed. The Secretary of State issued an apology to the applicant for the inconvenience caused by the delay and paid her GBP 10,381.14. Mr K alleged that he had stopped paying as two of the qualifying children had been living with him for [DATE_TIME] had moved in recently, while the fourth had gone to live with the mother in [LOCATION]. The CSA was aware of the changed circumstances of the children and had taken this into account in assessments. Mr K again stopped paying. EOs on the company of which he was a director proved unsuccessful. Arrears remained due however and the CSA continued to seek to enforce them. The applicant brought proceedings under the Human Rights Act (HRA) seeking a declaration that the provisions of the Child Support Act (CSA) were incompatible with Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The claimant believed that she would not have received a fraction of the money eventually paid if she had not continually pressurised the CSA and complained of their inaction. Mr Justice [PERSON] found that the applicant had a civil right to seek maintenance for her children from their father, such right being an autonomous substantive right, plainly recognised in English law and provided for by domestic legislation. The exclusion of the claimant from the enforcement process imposed a procedural bar on the prosecution/enforcement of the claim which engaged Article 6. On this basis the scheme under the [DATE_TIME] Act was HRA compliant. He issued directions with a view to an eventual trial as to whether there had been undue delay and to determine any damages. House of Lords, by a majority of four to one, rejected the applicant’s appeal. The state has an interest, most directly in cases where public funds are disbursed, but also more generally that children should be adequately supported. The [DATE_TIME] Act cannot in my opinion be interpreted as conferring any right on a parent in the position of Mrs [K]. She is of course the person to whom child maintenance will be paid, directly or indirectly and subject to any deduction of benefit. But the right which she had enjoyed under the former legislation was removed, and the right to recover the maintenance has been vested in the CSA. The obligation of a parent to maintain his children and the right of the children to have the benefit of the parental obligation to maintain them were not wholly contained in the [DATE_TIME] Act. The new scheme which transferred the task of assessing and collecting maintenance from the courts did not however remove these obligations. The children’s civil right to parental support survived. The Government did not want to create one law for the rich and one for the poor. There were also cases where the parent with care was sometimes in receipt of benefits and at other times not. She concluded that this was just the sort of policy choice in a socio-economic field which the courts were usually prepared to leave to Parliament.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28291/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the application was joined to the other applications (Rule 43): 26480/95, 29280/95,. 26699/96,. 29700/96, 29701/96 and 29702/96. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. It referred the case to the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court. The applicant appealed the decision and the case is now before the Court of cassation. The case is being heard by the Turkish Court of Appeal. The application is expected to be heard in early 2015.

He also joined an action for damages to the private prosecution and sought compensation. The District Court put to the jury 66 questions relating to the articles published in Expressen. The jury found that certain published statements or pictures amounted to defamation of a normal degree. The court then had to make a re-assessment of liability. The contravening statements were the following: “He is pointed out as PALME’s MURDERER” [“[NRP] pekas ut som PALMES MÖRDARE”] together with a picture of the applicant. “In addition to Long reach, [PERSON] and White had several companies together, some with links to the Mafia. Among others, the GMR Group in the [LOCATION] which was used for laundering money from illegal activities.” The text on page 6: “White has been dealing with most things. and drugs are two products that have been mentioned. – He is one of southern [LOCATION]’s biggest poachers, tells a source. It is to a large degree his fault that the elephants in [ LOCATION] are all but extinct.” [“White har sysslat med det mesta. – [NRP] är en av södra Afrikas [PERSON], [LOCation] en källa. Det Är till stor [Person] i Mocambique år så gott som utrotade”] [Aftonbladet, [DATE_TIME]. The Court of Appeal finds, like the District Court, that the relevant information in Expressen and Aftonbladet depicts [PERSON] as a criminal and as having a reprehensible lifestyle. The information has been liable to expose him to the contempt of others and consequently, as such, constitutes defamation. The question then is whether there are grounds for excluding liability. If the information is correct it may as a rule be communicated even if it is deprecatory, if this is justifiable with reference to the public news interest. There is no general right always to speak the truth if the statements are offensive. A balance has to be struck between the protection against offensive statements and the demands of freedom of speech. The Court of Appeal agrees with the District Court’s assessment that it was obviously legitimate to write about the so-called “[LOCATION] trail’ and to present information in this regard. The question is whether it was justified to identify the plaintiff by name and picture in the manner employed and to publish statements to the effect that he was supposed to be guilty of large scale, serious criminality. Aftonbladet, for its part, has asserted that, in the circumstances, it was justifiable to describe [PERSON]’S personality and conduct. The information in the case reveals that [Person] has been much better known than he has wished to admit. The Court of Appeal concludes that the responsible editors have not shown that the disseminated information was correct. The fact that the information had already been published by other media shows, however, that these news services might have considered that there was a reasonable basis for the information. In their defence, [the responsible editors] have also pointed out that, despite time constraints, they had careful checks made which gave an unequivocal picture of [PERSON]. A balance has to be struck between the protection against offensive statements and the demands of freedom of speech. Court of Appeal agrees with the District Court’s assessment that it was obviously legitimate to write about the so-called “[LOCATION] trail’ The question is whether it was justified to identify the plaintiff by name and picture in the manner employed and to publish statements to the effect that he was supposed to be guilty of large scale, serious criminality. In so finding, the Court of Appeal has also taken into account that [PERSON] had declined to comment on information presented by the journalists of Aftonbladet. With respect to the question of whether the information is correct, it is word against word. The Court of Appeal concludes that Expressen and Aftonbladet have not shown that the disseminated information was correct. The fact that the information had already been published by other media shows, however, that these news services might have considered that there was a reasonable basis for the information. It has been established that the main basis. for the assertions in issue in the case was the statements made by [the former senior. official of the [NRP] security police] [PERSON] and that the newspapers checked that. information mainly by having the journalists who wrote the articles contact. colleagues, public servants [and] representatives of various organisations for the. protection of animals and the conservation of nature. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was communicated to the Government on [DATE_TIME]. The applicants own property close to [LOCATION], in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, the [NRP] network of nature protection areas established under the EU Habitats Directive. Six of the present applicants own houses or land within the mentioned “corridor’. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment in a Natura 2000 area. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted [NRP] law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. The closest piece of land is located about 50 metres from the “Corridor”. The distance from their properties to the ‘corridor' or the specific stretch of the railway fixed in later proceedings vary; the houses appear to be situated 300 – 2500 metres away. The plan on compensation measures had to be presented to Government before the railway plan was adopted. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in [LOCATION] Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. Also applied to Environmental Court (miljödomstolen) in Umeå for permits to build two bridges. Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. Environmental Court of Appeal quashed the Environmental Court’s judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. The court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. The NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. All applicants except Mr [PERSON] appealed against the part which concerned the permit to construct the bridges. name: Oliver Riepan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35115/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing as the trial was held in the prison where he was detained. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to hold the hearing at [LOCATION], which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel. The Government were unable to provide the list for [DATE_TIME], as these lists are not kept, but asserted that it would, in accordance with the usual practice, have indicated [ LOCATION] as the place. The hearing list was distributed by the public prosecutor's office to the media, namely to the most important national and regional newspapers and to the national broadcasting station. On [DATE_TIME] the Steyr Regional Court, sitting with a single judge, held a hearing in the closed area of Garsten Prison. There is disagreement between the parties as to whether there were further seats available for witnesses and potential spectators. Neither the applicant nor his counsel complained about a lack of publicity at that time. Following the hearing, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of threatening behaviour, finding that he had on three occasions threatened prison personnel with arson or assault. He was sentenced to imprisonment. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe). He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing had not been public since it took place in a closed area. The Court of Appeal dismissed the case. It did not rehear the witnesses and the defence made no request to this effect. As to the complaint that the hearing on [DATE_TIME] had not been public, the court noted that, according to information submitted by the Steyr Regional Court, the hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. In any case, no such persons wishing to attend the trial had been present at the beginning of the hearing, and the judge had not was informed of any potential spectators. Finally, it found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt.

name: Gerhard Klass
train_texts: The case of Klass and others was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in an application against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention. The purpose of the request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 1, [Date_TIME) and 13 ( art. 6-1, art. 8, 13) The President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. The Government filed a memorial with the Court of Appeal on 10 August. The Court gave the Delegates of the Commission until 12 August to file a reply. The hearing was to start on 13 August and was to last for four days. The Government gave the Court the power to grant or deny permission to speak. The decision was reached after a meeting in private between the Government and the Commission. The case is currently before the Supreme Court of Justice, which will decide whether to grant the Government’s request for permission to give a statement in French or in English. The President of the European Court of Human Rights will decide on whether or not to grant permission for the use of English. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. [PERSON] for the Government and by Mr. [ PERSON] and Mr.  [P/) for the Commission. The applicants claim that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) and a statute enacted in pursuance of that provision are contrary to the Convention. They do not dispute that the State has the right to have recourse to the surveillance measures contemplated by the legislation. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities in every case to notify the persons concerned after the event. Their application is directed against the legislation as modified and interpreted by the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany were prompted by this judgment to propose amendments to the G 10. Although, as a precautionary measure, the applicants claimed before both the Constitutional Court and the Commission that they were being subjected to surveillance measures, they did not know whether the G Ten had actually been applied to them. There is also no question of the applicants’ having been indirectly involved in a surveillance measure directed against another person - at least, not in any fashion which would have permitted their identification. Neither as persons suspected of one or more of the offences specified in the Act nor as third parties within the meaning of Article 1, paragraph 2, sub-paragraph 2, of the G10 have the applicants been subjected to such measures. The Government introduced two Bills as part of the Emergency Legislation. The first sought primarily to amend Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law; the second was designed to limit the right to secrecy of the mail, post and telecommunications. The Government wished to substitute the domestic law for the rights exercised by the Three Powers and to place under legal control interferences with the right, guaranteed by Article 10 of thebasic law, to respect for correspondence. The two Acts, having been adopted by the federal legislative assemblies, were enacted on [DATE_TIME] and [D date_TIME) respectively. The Three Powers had come to the view that these two texts met the requirements of Article 5 para.2 of the above-mentioned Convention. Their statements declared: “The rights of the Three powers heretofore held or exercised by them which which were to lapse.“ Secrecy of the mail, post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. Restrictions may be ordered only pursuant to a statute. Where restrictions are intended to protect the free democratic constitutional order or the existence or security of the Federation or of a Land, the statute may provide that the person concerned shall not be notified of the restriction. The legal remedy through the courts shall be replaced by a system of scrutiny by agencies and auxiliary agencies appointed by the people’s elected representatives.“The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies (in Article 1 para. 1) the cases in which the competent authorities may impose the restrictions provided for in that paragraph. The Act provides that an application for surveillance measures may be made only by the head, or his substitute, of one of the following services: the Agencies for the Protection of the Constitution of the Federation and the Länder. The measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. Measures remain in force for a maximum of [DATE_TIME] and may be renewed only on fresh application (Article 1 para. 5, sub-paragraph 3). The G 10 Commission is responsible for supervising the application of surveillance measures. The Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If the Commission declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. The Minister is bound every month to provide the Commission with an account of the measures he has ordered. In practice and except in urgent cases, the minister seeks the prior consent of this Commission. The Government, moreover, intend proposing to Parliament to amend the G 10 so as to make such prior consent obligatory. According to Article 1 para. 9, sub-paragraph 5, of the G 10: “... there shall be no legal remedy before the courts in respect of the ordering and implementation of restrictive measures.“ For the Länder, their legislatures lay down the parliamentary supervision to which the supreme authorities are subject in the matter. The G 10 Commission draws up its own rules of procedure which must be approved by the Board; before taking this decision, the Board consults the Government. For the (above-)mentioned reasons ..., the person concerned is deprived of the opportunity of having the restrictive measures ordered examined by a court. The present [PERSON] grants the power of decision to a Federal Minister or the supreme authority of the Land. A person who has applied to the G 10 Commission without success retains the right to apply to the Constitutional Court. The court may reject the application on the ground that the applicant is unable to adduce proof to substantiate a complaint. It may also request the Government concerned to supply it with information or to produce documents to enable it to verify for itself the individual’s allegations. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. The Constitutional Court may decide by a two-thirds majority that their use is incompatible with State security and dismiss the application. The Agent of the Government admitted that this remedy might be employed only on rare occasions. In their application lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME], the applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 empower the authorities to monitor their correspondence and telephone communications. The Commission declared the application admissible. It found, as regards Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention: “... only the victim of an alleged violation may bring an application.” The Commission is still of the opinion ... that the applicants must be considered as if they were victims. Some of the applicants are barristers and it is theoretically excluded that they are in fact subject to secret surveillance in consequence of contacts they may have with clients who are suspected of anti-constitutional activities. The Commission then expressed the opinion that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention insofar as the applicants relied on the notion “civil rights’ The report contains various separate opinions. The Commission also expressed its opinion that there was no breach of Articles 8 or 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application was inadmissible, according to the Commission's conclusion. The Government's Agent of the Government said the application was 'inadmissible' and that the Court should find that [LOCATION] had not violated the Convention. The Court is expected to rule on the application on November 25.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29912/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. name: Snjezana Vostic
train_texts: The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that the court decisions in compensation proceedings for detention on remand violated the presumption of innocence. On [DATE_TIME] the Wels Regional Court (Landesgericht) remanded the applicant in custody on suspicion of murder. The jury answered the main question as to murder with six votes ‘no’ and two votes “yes’ The jury gave the following reasons for its decision: “The evidence produced produced the evidence produced by the applicant.” The applicant requested compensation for her detention on remand. The Wels Regional Court, with the same composition as above, dismissed the applicant’s claim. It found that, apart from the fact that the jury's verdict had not been unanimous, the suspicion against the applicant had not be dispelled. The decision was served on the applicant after her acquittal had become final on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) She argued that section 2 (1)(b) of the [D date_TIME] Act was incompatible with Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. Furthermore, the main suspicion against her had been dispelled during the trial and her defence that she had no contact with the victim had been disproved. Court of Appeal: Prosecution cannot refuse a claim on the grounds that suspicion has not been dispelled. The trial court held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to [DATE_TIME], was not credible. The Court of Appeal continued as follows: “Nor does the principle of the presumption of innocence prevent the prosecuting authorities from suspecting someone of having committed an offence’” The court ruled that the prosecution had not fully dispelled a ‘persisting’ suspicion concerning [PERSON] that had not been wholly dispelled, particularly in view of the fact that it was still possible that [Person] gun had been the murder weapon.
